Newness
nu'nes
n. (the state of being new; novelty; freshness of life or spirit)
From new, Saxon niwe, with the noun-ending -ness. Twice in the Authorized Version, both in Romans, and both describing the manner of a Christian's living rather than the date of his conversion.

Biblical Definition

Both occurrences belong to Paul and both stand at the hinge of the Christian life. The first is the fruit of union with Christ in His death and resurrection: “Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life” (Rom 6:4). Note the logic. The newness is not an improvement bolted onto the old man; it is the walking that follows a burial. The old man was crucified with Him (Rom 6:6), and what walks out is new. The second occurrence contrasts two ways of serving God: “that we should serve in newness of spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter” (Rom 7:6). The Christian is not a Pharisee with better manners; he serves from a changed nature, not from an external code held over a dead heart. Paul states the same doctrine as a verdict in 2 Corinthians: “Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new” (2Co 5:17). Newness in Scripture is therefore always derived — it comes out of a grave, and it is Christ's resurrection life expressing itself in a man's ordinary Tuesday.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines newness as lateness of origin; recentness; novelty; innovation; and also a different state or qualities introduced by change or regeneration.

expand to see more

NEW'NESS, n.

1. Lateness of origin; recentness; state of being lately invented or produced; as the newness of a dress.

2. Novelty; the state of being first known or introduced.

3. Innovation; recent change.

4. Want of practice or familiarity. 5. Different state or qualities introduced by change or regeneration. That we should walk in newness of life. Rom. 6.

Key Scripture

Romans 6:4 — "Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life."

Romans 7:6 — "But now we are delivered from the law, that being dead wherein we were held; that we should serve in newness of spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter."

Romans 6:6 — "Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin."

2 Corinthians 5:17 — "Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new."

Modern Corruption

Newness is preached as a fresh start the sinner makes rather than a resurrection life he is given.

expand to see more

The revivalist tradition has long offered newness as a turning over of a new leaf — a decision, a rededication, a clean page in January. Romans 6:4 puts a funeral between the old and the new. There is no new walking that does not come out of a burial with Christ, and a man who has not died with Him has not begun. This is why Reformed teaching insists regeneration precedes faith: the newness is not the reward of the sinner's effort but the cause of his believing.

The therapeutic version is subtler. It reads 2 Corinthians 5:17 as a promise about self-perception — you are a new creature, so think better of yourself — when Paul is making an objective statement about a man's standing and nature in Christ, not a suggestion about his self-image. And Romans 7:6 blocks the opposite ditch, where newness becomes an excuse to despise the law altogether. The Christian is delivered from the law as a covenant of works; he is not delivered into lawlessness. He serves — that verb stays — but in newness of spirit.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek kainotes (G2538), newness of kind; kainos (G2537), new in quality as opposed to neos, new in time.

expand to see more

Greek kainotes (G2538) — newness; both Romans 6:4 and 7:6 use this noun and no other place does.

Greek kainos (G2537) — new in kind, fresh in nature; distinguished from neos (G3501), new merely in time.

Greek palaiotes (G3821) — oldness; the deliberate opposite in Romans 7:6, the letter grown stale.

Greek kaine ktisis (G2537, G2937) — new creature, new creation; 2 Corinthians 5:17.

Saxon niwe — new; Webster's root, and the -ness that makes the adjective a state.

Usage

"“Walk in newness of life” — walking, which is daily, out of a burial, which was once."

"“Newness of spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter” — the service continues; the power changes."

"“He is a new creature” — a statement of fact, not a suggestion about self-image."
